newsitem.title: UK: Bowel disease going undiagnosed, conference told.
newsitem.headline: Bowel disease going undiagnosed, conference told.

text.p: Bowel disorders such as coeliac disease and Crohn's disease, which can lead to deadly bowel cancer, are going undiagnosed, British experts said on Tuesday.
They told a meeting of the Royal Society of Gastroenterology that better screening and diagnosis could save many people from embarrassment, misery and possible death.

"Although there are approximately 36,000 diagnosed coeliacs in the UK, we now believe that for every one coeliac diagnosed there are possibly four remaining undiagnosed," Paul Ciclitira of London's St Thomas' Hospital told the meeting.
Coeliac disease is an intolerance of gluten, the protein that gives bread its body and which is found in wheat, oats and other grains. Symptoms vary but include diarrhoea, weight loss and anaemia.
The only way to diagnose it is by endoscopic biopsy -- inserting a tiny camera into the bowel to help take a sample. But Ciclitira said he was working on a blood test.

Richard Logan and colleagues at the University of Nottingham told the conference they had examined 45,000 people and found 57 cases of previously undiagnosed inflammatory bowel disease, a broad group of digestive disorders that kill 300 people a year in Britain.
Logan said this figure, which included Crohn's disease victims, was much higher than expected.

"Inflammatory bowel disease remains a serious problem for a number of reasons," commented Rodney Taylor of the British Society of Gastroenterology. "Delayed diagnosis and late referral of urgent cases allow the patient's condition to deteriorate."
He added: "The disease can rapidly progress, carrying the risk of longer-term complications including bowel cancer."
They urged quick testing of anyone who had blood in their faeces or general abdominal complaints.
